title: Butterscotch fudge
subtitle: a rich brown sugar and butter fudge with a caramel depth and smooth, yielding texture
excerpt: Butterscotch fudge is made from brown sugar, butter, and cream cooked to the soft-ball stage and beaten as it cools to develop the smooth, yielding texture of traditional fudge. Brown sugar gives a deeper caramel flavour than white. The beating is the critical step: it breaks down the sugar crystals and makes the fudge smooth rather than grainy.
sourceNotes: Fudge as a confection is thought to have originated in the United States in the late nineteenth century, with Scottish tablet as a related British precedent. Butterscotch flavouring using brown sugar and butter has been a feature of British confectionery since at least the nineteenth century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.

content.text: Butterscotch fudge is brown sugar, butter, and cream cooked together to the soft-ball stage, then beaten until smooth as it cools. The soft-ball stage (114 to 116 degrees C) gives the fudge its yielding, melt-in-the-mouth texture rather than the hard, crumbly tablet texture of a higher temperature. The beating introduces tiny sugar crystals that make the fudge smooth rather than grainy.

Line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper. Put the brown sugar, butter, cream, and milk in a medium heavy-based saucepan. Heat over low heat, stirring, until the sugar has dissolved and the butter has melted. Do not let it boil until the sugar is fully dissolved.
Clip on the sugar thermometer and bring to the boil. Cook over medium heat, stirring regularly, until the mixture reaches 115 degrees C (soft-ball stage). This takes around 15 to 20 minutes.
Remove from the heat. Add the vanilla extract. Leave to cool without stirring for 10 minutes until the base of the pan is comfortable to touch but the fudge is still warm.

Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon or electric hand mixer for 5 to 8 minutes. The mixture will thicken, turn paler brown, and lose its glossy shine. When it holds a thick trail when dropped from the spoon, it is ready to pour.
Pour into the prepared tin and spread level. Scatter flaked salt on top if using. Leave to set at room temperature for 2 hours, or refrigerate for 1 hour.
Turn out and cut into squares with a sharp knife. Store in an airtight container at room temperature.

attrs.problem: Fudge grainy and crystalline rather than smooth
attrs.avoid: Avoid stirring the mixture while it is boiling up to temperature; this introduces premature crystallisation.
attrs.fix: Stir only to prevent sticking while heating. Once at temperature and removed from the heat, wait the full 10 minutes before beating. Beating too early, while too hot, also causes graininess.

attrs.problem: Fudge does not set and stays soft or sticky
attrs.avoid: Avoid undercooking; if the temperature does not reach 114 to 116 degrees C, the fudge will not set properly.
attrs.fix: Return the mixture to the saucepan and cook again to the correct temperature. The set fudge can be remelted and re-cooked if needed.
